text: A sum of two independent Poisson processes is again a Poisson process, with rate lambda one plus lambda two. So the chance of exactly four customers in the first hour is e to the minus lambda one plus lambda two times lambda one plus lambda two to the fourth over four factorial. If four arrived in total, the chance that they all went to store one should be lambda one over lambda one plus lambda two raised to some power, probably the fourth, but I am not sure how to show it. I did not cover the exponential time T part.

The stationary distribution is found by solving G times pi equals zero with pi as a column, and no normalisation is needed. Since both four state chains have the same number of states the stationary distribution is uniform, one quarter in each state. In the taxi chain the limiting probability of waiting at location one is one half, because the driver is at one of the two locations.

For a birth death process with birth rates lambda n and death rates beta n, it is transient exactly when the sum over n of beta n down to beta one over lambda n down to lambda one is finite. It is positive recurrent, which is the same as having a stationary distribution, exactly when the sum of lambda n minus one down to lambda zero over beta n down to beta one is finite. When both sums are infinite the process is null recurrent. With lambda n equal to one plus one over n plus one and beta n equal to one, the first sum behaves like the sum of n plus one and the second like the sum of two over n plus two, both infinite, so it is null recurrent. With lambda n equal to one minus one over n plus two, again both sums are infinite, so null recurrent. In the last exercise the sum is the sum of one over n factorial, which is e minus one and finite, so the process is positive recurrent, with pi zero equal to one over e and pi n equal to one over n factorial times e.

In the first chain the sojourn time in state one is exponential with rate three, so the expected time before it first changes state is one third. For the time to reach state four I invert minus G and multiply by a vector of ones, which gives about one. In the second chain the sojourn time in state one is exponential with rate two, so the expected time is one half. I did not finish the hitting time for the second chain.

For birth death processes there are two sums to check. A process is positive recurrent, so it has a stationary distribution, exactly when the sum of lambda n minus one down to lambda zero over beta n down to beta one is finite. It is transient when a similar sum is finite, I think the one with the rates the other way up. I did not go through the null recurrent cases or the one over n factorial exercise.

The sales are a Poisson process with rate six per hour, since twenty arrivals times point three, so over eight hours the expected number of sales is forty eight. The time until the first sale is exponential with mean one sixth of an hour, so about ten past ten. For ten or more sales in an hour I would add up the Poisson probabilities, but I do not remember the number. For the last part, I think what happened in the first hour does not matter much for the second hour, but I would not say it is exactly independent.

Customers arrive at twenty per hour and every one of them counts as a sale, so sales are Poisson with rate twenty and the expected number of sales in an eight hour day is one hundred sixty. The first sale takes on average one twentieth of an hour, three minutes, so the first sale is expected at ten oh three. If six sales happened in the first hour then the next hour has to catch up, so the chance of two or fewer sales next hour is smaller than usual.

Two independent exponential waiting times with rates lambda one and lambda two. The probability that the first is smaller is lambda one over lambda one plus lambda two. The minimum of the two is also exponential, I think, but I do not remember what its rate is. For the queue problem I did not work out the probability that customer A is still in service.

Customers come at twenty per hour and each one buys with probability point three, so sales are a Poisson process with rate twenty times point three, which is six per hour. In an eight hour day the expected number of sales is forty eight. The chance of ten or more sales in one hour is one minus the sum from n equals zero to nine of e to the minus six, six to the n, over n factorial. That is one minus point nine one six one, so about point zero eight three nine. The time until the first sale is exponential with mean one sixth of an hour, which is ten minutes, so if the store opens at ten the expected first sale is at ten ten. And if six sales happened in the first hour, that tells me nothing about the next hour, so the chance of two or fewer sales in the next hour is the same as the chance of two or fewer in one hour, which comes to about point zero six two.

A birth death process is positive recurrent when the sum of beta n down to beta one over lambda n down to lambda one is finite, and it is transient when the sum of lambda n minus one down to lambda zero over beta n down to beta one is finite. In the last exercise the sum of one over n factorial equals e minus one, which is finite, so the process is transient and has no stationary distribution. With lambda n equal to n plus two over n plus one and beta n equal to one, the process is positive recurrent.

In the first chain, state one has a total exit rate of three, so the sojourn time in state one is exponential with rate three and the expected time until the first change of state is one third. To get the expected time to reach state four I take minus G with the row and column for state four removed, invert it, and multiply by a vector of ones. For that chain I get a vector of ones, so starting in state one it takes one unit of time on average. In the second chain the sojourn time in state one is exponential with rate two, so the expected time is one half, and the same recipe gives the vector four, four, three, so starting from state one the expected time to reach state four is four.

Say there are two independent clocks, one for each store, with exponential times T-X with rate lambda one and T-Y with rate lambda two. The chance that store one rings first is lambda one over lambda one plus lambda two. The time of the very first ring, the minimum of the two, is also exponential, and its rate is lambda one plus lambda two, so the rates add. For the two server problem, P-A is the chance that X-one is smaller than X-two. I condition on X-one being equal to t. Given that, X-two has to be bigger than t, which has probability e to the minus lambda two t. Then I integrate lambda one e to the minus lambda one t times e to the minus lambda two t, and I get lambda one over lambda one plus lambda two.

If the two stores have independent Poisson processes, X with rate lambda one and Y with rate lambda two, then X of t plus Y of t is again a Poisson process, and its rate is lambda one plus lambda two. So the chance that exactly four customers arrive at the two stores in the first hour is e to the minus lambda one plus lambda two, times lambda one plus lambda two to the fourth, over four factorial. If I am told four arrived in total, the chance that all four went to store one is lambda one over lambda one plus lambda two, all to the fourth power. I get it by writing the event as X of one equals four and Y of one equals zero, and using independence. Finally, if T is exponential with rate lambda two, the chance that store one has k arrivals by time T is lambda two over lambda one plus lambda two, times lambda one over lambda one plus lambda two to the k. I get that by integrating the Poisson probability against the density of T.

For the barbershop the stationary distribution is uniform, one third in each of the three states, because the shop has three states. The average number of customers in the shop is one, and two thirds of potential customers enter. If the barber works twice as fast nothing changes, because customers still arrive at three per hour, so the business does not grow at all. In the other birth death example the proportion of time the population is at least three is about one half.

To find the stationary distribution of a finite continuous time Markov chain I solve pi times G equals zero, the balance equations, and then normalise so the probabilities add up to one. For the first four state example the answer I got was pi equals three, seven, nine, nineteen divided by thirty eight, and for the second example it was one, three, two, two divided by eight.

For the generator G with first row minus one, one and second row four, minus four, the transition matrix is P of t equals e to the t G. Working it out, the first row is four fifths plus one fifth e to the minus five t, and one fifth minus one fifth e to the minus five t. The second row is four fifths minus four fifths e to the minus five t, and one fifth plus four fifths e to the minus five t. For the disability model with healthy, disabled and dead, I solve Kolmogorov's forward equations numerically with Euler's forward method and step size point one. In the first step p zero zero of point one is one minus point zero zero six, so point nine nine four, and p zero one of point one is point one times point zero five, so point zero zero five. After the second step p zero one of point two is point zero zero nine nine two, and p zero zero of point two is point nine nine four squared, which is point nine eight eight zero three six.

In the birth death example with birth rate n plus one up to state two and n after that, and death rate two n, I add up the earlier balance equations and get minus n plus one pi n plus one plus two n plus two pi n plus two equals zero, so pi n plus two is n plus one over two times n plus two, times pi n plus one. That gives pi zero about point five one one six six, and the proportion of time the population is at least three is one minus pi zero minus pi one minus pi two, about point one zero four six. For the barbershop with arrivals at three per hour and mean service time a quarter hour, the states are zero, one, two, with q one zero and q two one both equal to four, and the stationary distribution is sixteen, twelve, nine over thirty seven. The average number of customers is pi one plus two pi two, thirty over thirty seven, and the proportion who enter is the fraction of time with zero or one customers, pi zero plus pi one, twenty eight over thirty seven. If the barber works twice as fast the distribution is sixty four, twenty four, nine over ninety seven, the entering proportion is eighty eight over ninety seven, and business grows by eighty eight over ninety seven divided by twenty eight over thirty seven, minus one, which is 19.88 percent.

Two independent clocks, store one with rate lambda one and store two with rate lambda two. The probability that store one rings first is lambda two over lambda one plus lambda two, because the clock with the bigger rate takes longer. The first ring of either clock is exponential with a rate equal to the smaller of lambda one and lambda two. For the queue, the chance that customer A is still in service is lambda two over lambda one plus lambda two.

Two independent exponential waiting times, one with rate lambda one and one with rate lambda two. The probability the first one is smaller is lambda one divided by lambda one plus lambda two. And the minimum of the two is exponential with rate equal to the sum, lambda one plus lambda two. In the queue example, customer A is still in service when I get to server two exactly when X-one is less than X-two. I condition on X-one equals t, and then X-two must exceed t, probability e to the minus lambda two t. Integrating gives lambda one over lambda one plus lambda two.

The stationary distribution pi of a finite state continuous time chain with generator G solves the balance equation pi G equals zero, together with a normalisation so the entries add to one. For the chain with rows minus three, one, one, one, then zero, minus three, two, one, then one, two, minus four, one, then zero, zero, one, minus one, the answer is pi equals three, seven, nine, nineteen all over thirty eight. For the chain with rows minus two, one, one, zero, then zero, minus one, one, zero, then one, one, minus three, one, then zero, zero, one, minus one, the answer is pi equals one, three, two, two over eight. In the taxi chain the state space is finite and irreducible, so the stationary distribution exists and is unique, and the limit of p i zero of t is pi zero, which is one over six point two, about point one six one two nine.
